desc:
You may delete edges of a binary tree, which splits it into several connected pieces. A set of deletions is good if every resulting piece contains an even number of nodes.

Return the maximum number of edges that can be deleted by a good set of deletions. The number of nodes in the tree is always even, so deleting nothing is a good set.

Only the shape of the tree matters, so every node in the input has value 0.

How trees are given. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order (top to bottom, left to right). The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn; a missing child is written as -1 (real node values are never negative). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped.

For example, [1,2,3,-1,4] is the tree whose root 1 has children 2 and 3; node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child; node 3 is a leaf.

Example 1

tree = [0,0,0,0]
Output: 1
The root has children a and b, and a has a left child c. Deleting the edge between the root and a leaves the pieces {a, c} and {root, b}, both of size 2.

Example 2

tree = [0,0,-1,0,-1,0,-1,0,-1,0]
Output: 2
A path of 6 nodes. Cutting after the 2nd and the 4th node leaves three pieces of size 2.
constraints: 2 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 3,000, and the number of nodes is even
The array follows the encoding above exactly
hints: Deleting the edge between a node and its parent cuts off exactly the subtree of that node. When is it allowed to cut there?

If the subtree of u has an even number of nodes, cutting above it creates an even piece, and the rest of the tree loses an even number of nodes, so it stays even in total. If the subtree is odd, cutting there can never be part of a good set.
Compute subtree sizes bottom-up and count the non-root nodes whose subtree size is even. Remember that the cuts do not interfere: every such edge can be deleted at the same time.
editorial: Count the nodes of every subtree: size[u] = 1 + size[l] + size[r]. Deleting the edge above u separates a piece of size size[u] from the rest, so it is only possible when size[u] is even in a good set. Conversely, delete the edges above all non-root nodes with even subtree size at once: every resulting piece is the subtree of such a node minus the subtrees of the even descendants cut below it, which is an even number minus even numbers, hence even. The root's piece is the total (even) minus even numbers, again even.
So the answer is the number of non-root nodes with an even subtree size. One backwards sweep over the level-order array gives O(n) time and O(n) memory.
